questions.stem: In a class discussion, Priya says: "I disagree with Marco's reading of the poem, because the final stanza describes the town as 'hollowed out', which suggests loss rather than hope." Which interaction skill is Priya using?
options: Summarising the group's shared conclusion for the class
Conceding a point in order to keep the discussion polite
Challenging an interpretation by citing evidence from the text
Clarifying the discussion topic by asking an open question
questions.explanation: Priya names the view she opposes and then supports her objection with a specific quotation, which is exactly what challenging a stated meaning with textual evidence looks like. "Conceding a point in order to keep the discussion polite" is tempting because her phrasing is courteous, but she does not accept Marco's view at all — she opposes it. The cue is the word 'disagree' followed by evidence: politeness of tone is separate from the function of the move.

questions.stem: What does it mean to challenge an *implied* meaning of a text in discussion?
options: Questioning an idea the text suggests without stating it directly
Pointing out a spelling or punctuation error in the text
Disagreeing with a sentence that appears word for word in the text
Objecting to the personal opinions of another student in the group
questions.explanation: An implied meaning is one the reader infers from clues such as word choice, imagery or what is left out, rather than one the text says outright. "Disagreeing with a sentence that appears word for word in the text" describes challenging a stated meaning, which is the contrast term, not the definition of implied. The cue is 'implied' = inferred and unstated; 'stated' = written on the page.
questions.teaching:
Texts carry two kinds of meaning, and challenging one is different from challenging the other.

Stated meaning is on the page — you can point to the sentence. Implied meaning is suggested without being said outright, through what is emphasised, what is omitted, which words are chosen, and what is treated as obvious. Challenging the implied kind means naming an idea the text conveys without stating and questioning it, which requires evidence for why you think it is there. That evidence requirement is what makes it an analytical move rather than an assertion.

questions.stem: Which contribution best *supports* another student's claim that a news article portrays the protesters sympathetically?
options: "That fits — the writer calls them 'concerned locals' rather than 'a mob'."
"I think protests are usually reported unfairly by most newspapers."
"I agree completely, and everyone in our group thinks the same thing."
"That's a good point, but the headline is printed in very large type."
questions.explanation: Genuine support builds on a claim by adding evidence from the text, here a contrast in labelling that shows sympathetic representation. "I agree completely, and everyone in our group thinks the same thing" is tempting because it sounds strongly supportive, but agreement plus a head count adds no evidence and does not develop the claim. Look for whether the contribution points back to something in the text.

questions.stem: A small group must reach a decision about which of two advertisements is more persuasive, in ten minutes. Which interaction skill is most suited to that purpose and context?
options: Keeping contributions brief and checking the group is on track
Delivering an uninterrupted prepared speech to state one's view
Allowing the discussion to drift so all interests are explored
Waiting silently until the strongest speaker settles the question
questions.explanation: Interaction skills are chosen to suit purpose and context; a short, decision-focused task calls for concise turns and monitoring of progress. "Allowing the discussion to drift so all interests are explored" sounds inclusive, but it defeats the stated purpose of reaching a decision within a time limit. Match the skill to the job: exploratory tasks reward wandering, decision tasks reward focus.

questions.stem: Ben claims a short story implies the narrator regrets leaving home. Which question from a group member most usefully tests that inference?
options: "Did you finish reading the whole story before class today?"
"Which details in the story led you to read regret into it?"
"Do you personally regret anything you've done recently?"
"Would you say the story was enjoyable or a bit boring?"
questions.explanation: Testing an inference means asking what textual evidence produced it, so the group can judge whether the implication is supported. "Do you personally regret anything you've done recently?" is tempting because it seems to build empathy, but it moves the discussion from the text to Ben's private life and tests nothing about the reading. The cue is that a probing question in text discussion should point back to the page.

questions.stem: Which pair of phrases both signal that a speaker is about to *qualify* rather than flatly reject a classmate's interpretation?
options: "To sum up our talk…" and "So the group has decided that…"
"I'd partly agree, although…" and "That works up to a point, but…"
"That's simply not right…" and "You've misread the whole text…"
"Building on that exactly…" and "I'd say precisely the same thing…"
questions.explanation: Qualifying language accepts part of a view while limiting it, which is what 'partly agree, although' and 'works up to a point, but' both do. "That's simply not right…" and "You've misread the whole text…" are tempting because they are also disagreement, but they are outright rejections with no concession, so they are not qualifications. Listen for a concession clause before the 'but'.

questions.stem: Two students disagree about whether a documentary is biased. Which move most improves the quality of the disagreement itself?
options: Asking the teacher to decide which student is actually right
Setting the question aside and moving to an easier segment
Agreeing first on what would count as evidence of bias
Each restating their original position more forcefully and clearly
questions.explanation: Productive disagreement needs shared criteria; once both agree what would count as evidence of bias, they can weigh the text against the same standard. "Each restating their original position more forcefully and clearly" is tempting because clarity matters, but repetition with more force adds no new grounds and usually hardens the deadlock. The cue is whether the move creates a way to settle the point using the text.

questions.stem: A group is discussing a persuasive letter. Which contribution challenges the letter's *implied* meaning rather than its stated claim?
options: "It states the plan will cost $80 million, and that figure is wrong."
"It says the council voted last March, but the vote was in April."
"It argues the plan should be stopped, and I disagree with stopping it."
"By listing only the costs, it hints the plan has no benefits at all."
questions.explanation: Challenging an implied meaning means questioning something the text suggests through selection or emphasis — here, the omission of benefits creating an unstated impression. "It argues the plan should be stopped, and I disagree with stopping it" is tempting because it is clear disagreement, but the letter states that argument openly, so the challenge is to a stated meaning. Ask yourself: is the idea printed, or produced by what the writer chose to leave out?

questions.stem: In a spoken presentation, what does a speaker's 'pace' refer to?
options: The attitude the voice conveys towards the topic
The speed at which the words are spoken
The loudness or softness of the voice
The highness or lowness of the voice
questions.explanation: Pace is the rate of delivery — how quickly or slowly a speaker moves through their words, often slowed at key points for emphasis. Describing it as the highness or lowness of the voice confuses pace with pitch, which is a separate feature. A quick cue: pace is measured in time, pitch is measured in how high or low a note sounds, and volume in how loud it is.
questions.teaching:
A speaker controls several features of delivery, and each has its own name.

Volume is how loud. Pitch is how high or low. Tone is the attitude conveyed. Pause is deliberate silence. Emphasis is stress placed on particular words. And one feature covers how fast the words come — slowing down for something important, speeding up to convey urgency. Naming the right feature matters when analysing a speech, because saying a speaker 'spoke well' says nothing about what they actually did.

questions.stem: You are giving a three-minute formal presentation to your class and a visiting teacher. Which language choice best suits that context?
options: "Anyway, birds — kinda sad, honestly, but let's get into it."
"This report examines three causes of the decline in local birdlife."
"So yeah, I'm gonna talk about birds and stuff that's happening."
"You guys already know what I reckon about the bird thing, right?"
questions.explanation: A formal context calls for standard English, complete sentences and a clear statement of what the talk will cover, which orients an audience that includes a visitor. The option beginning "So yeah" may feel natural and friendly, but contractions like "gonna" and vague fillers like "and stuff" belong to informal conversation and leave the audience unsure of the topic. Test register by asking whether the wording would look out of place written in a report.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of 'signposting' language such as "First, I'll outline the problem; then I'll suggest two solutions" in a spoken text?
options: It proves the speaker's claims are supported by reliable evidence
It makes the speaker's tone sound more emotional and persuasive
It replaces the need for an introduction and a conclusion
It tells the audience how the talk is structured so they can follow it
questions.explanation: Signposting maps the structure aloud, because listeners cannot skim back the way readers can re-read a page. Saying it proves claims are supported confuses structural signalling with evidence — signposting says where you are going, not why you are right. If a phrase could be replaced by a heading in a written text, it is signposting.

questions.stem: Near the end of a persuasive speech, a student wants the audience to feel the weight of her final appeal. Which combination of vocal features would best achieve this?
options: Speeding up and raising volume steadily through the whole closing
Dropping to a near-whisper and reading the closing from a script
Keeping pace, pitch and volume flat so the words speak for themselves
Slowing the pace and pausing briefly before the closing sentence
questions.explanation: A deliberate slowing plus a short pause marks the closing as important and gives listeners a moment to absorb it, which is why speakers use it at climaxes. Speeding up while getting louder can read as panic or hectoring, and it flattens emphasis by making everything loud. Emphasis comes from contrast, so the feature that differs from your normal delivery is the one the audience notices.

questions.stem: Two students present the same research. One speaks to a Year 8 assembly, the other to a small group of friends at lunch. Which difference between the two spoken texts is most predictable?
options: The assembly talk uses shorter sentences and more slang for a bigger crowd
The lunchtime talk needs stronger evidence because friends are more critical
The lunchtime talk requires more projection because the room is noisier
The assembly talk uses more formal register and clearer structural signposting
questions.explanation: A large, mixed, public audience calls for formal register and explicit structure, since listeners cannot interrupt to ask where the talk is going. Claiming the assembly talk would use more slang reverses the relationship between audience formality and word choice. Ask who the audience is and how public the setting is: the more public, the more formal and the more signposted.

questions.stem: A student's talk aims to persuade the school council to fund a bike shelter. Which opening best matches that purpose and audience?
options: "I wasn't sure what to talk about, so I picked something to do with bikes."
"Forty-two students ride to school, and none of them have anywhere dry to park."
"Today I'm going to tell you everything I found out about bicycles in Australia."
"Bikes are honestly the best, and I've loved riding since I was about six."
questions.explanation: A persuasive talk to decision-makers should open with a specific problem stated in terms they can act on, which frames everything that follows as a case for funding. The option promising "everything I found out about bicycles" signals an informative survey with no argument and no request, so it misses the persuasive purpose. Check the opening against the purpose: persuasion needs a problem and a stake, not a topic announcement.

questions.stem: A student plans a talk on local flood risk and wants to use a short video clip. Which use of the clip best integrates a digital element into a structured spoken text?
options: A clip played at the very end after the speaker has finished and sat down
A 30-second clip of the 2022 flood, introduced and then unpacked by the speaker
A four-minute news report played at the start while the speaker sets up notes
A silent loop of flood footage running behind the speaker for the whole talk
questions.explanation: An integrated digital element is short, framed by the speaker beforehand and interpreted afterwards, so it advances the argument rather than interrupting it. Playing a four-minute news report at the start hands the talk over to someone else's voice and leaves the speaker's own structure undeveloped. The test is whether you can say in one sentence what the clip proves and where it fits in your sequence.

questions.stem: Ilias is preparing slides to accompany a five-minute formal presentation to his class on renewable energy. Which slide plan best supports a structured spoken text?
options: All graphs and images gathered onto one final slide, displayed once the spoken sections are finished
A few key words plus one labelled graph per slide, each introduced at the point in the talk it explains
The full script of the talk in small print on every slide, so each sentence can be read aloud accurately
A different font, colour scheme and animation on every slide, so the audience stays visually interested
questions.explanation: A multimodal element supports a spoken text when it carries information the voice cannot easily carry, and appears at the moment the speaker needs it, so the audience follows one idea at a time. Putting the full script on the slides is tempting because it feels safe, but the audience then reads ahead instead of listening, and the speaker loses eye contact and vocal expression — the slide replaces the talk rather than supporting it. The cue is integration: ask whether the visual is timed to a point in your structure, or just stored alongside it.

questions.stem: A short story published in 1954 describes an Australian country town where 'the men gathered at the pub while the women met at the hall'. What does this representation most likely reflect?
options: A signal that the story was written mainly for young children rather than for adult readers
Expectations about men's and women's roles that were widely held in Australian communities at that time
Factual errors by the writer, since country towns of the 1950s had many other public buildings
Evidence that the writer personally disapproved of country pubs and wanted readers to avoid them
questions.explanation: The detail divides the community by gender in a way that matches widely held mid-century assumptions about where men and women belonged, so the representation carries the values of its period. The 'factual errors' option treats a selective representation as a complete inventory of the town — writers choose details for effect, not to catalogue every building. Ask what the selection suggests about the values of the time, not whether it lists everything.

questions.stem: A tourism brochure describes a coastal town as 'a golden, unspoilt escape', while a local newspaper report on the same town focuses on eroding dunes and damaged sea walls. What best explains the difference?
options: One text is factual while the other is fictional, so only one can be describing the real town
The brochure writer must have visited the town more recently than the newspaper reporter did
The longer of the two texts will inevitably give the more accurate picture of the town
Each representation of the town is shaped by the purpose the text serves and the audience it addresses
questions.explanation: Both texts are non-fiction, but a brochure exists to attract visitors while a news report exists to inform residents about a local problem, so each selects different details of the same place. The fiction option is simply untrue: a tourism brochure is not fiction, it is persuasive non-fiction. When two texts describe one place differently, check purpose and audience before assuming one is lying.

questions.stem: A student argues that a novel's representation of a city reflects the economic hardship of the 1980s. Which piece of evidence best supports that argument?
options: The publisher's note stating that the author was born and raised in that same city
Repeated descriptions of boarded-up factories and long queues outside the employment office
The narrator's use of first person throughout, which makes the account feel immediate and personal
The novel's length of just over three hundred pages, divided into unusually short chapters
questions.explanation: To link a representation to its context you need textual details that carry the marks of that context — closed factories and dole queues are exactly such details. The author's birthplace is tempting because it sounds like contextual information, but it says nothing about how the city is portrayed on the page. Strong contextual analysis quotes what the text actually shows, then connects it to the period.

questions.stem: A picture book published in 2020 shows a busy Melbourne street where children of many backgrounds walk to school past halal grocers, a Vietnamese bakery and a bilingual library sign. What does this representation of place most clearly reflect about the text's context?
options: The cultural diversity of contemporary Australian urban life
The author's personal preference for writing about food and shops
The historical fact that Melbourne has always had these exact businesses
The requirement that picture books must include multiple languages
questions.explanation: The selected details — varied businesses, languages and children — build a representation that reflects the multicultural character of Australian cities in the present day, which is the text's context. Saying Melbourne 'has always had these exact businesses' is false: this diversity reflects particular waves of migration rather than an unchanging past. Look for what the chosen details say about the values and make-up of the society the text comes from.

questions.stem: Two accounts of the same 1850s goldfields camp survive: a letter from a British digger describing 'empty country waiting to be claimed', and an oral history from a local Aboriginal community describing Country that was farmed, fished and cared for. What is the best conclusion about these representations?
options: The oral history must be less reliable because it was not written down at the time
The letter must be more accurate because it was written by an eyewitness on the site
The two accounts must describe two different places, since they cannot both be about one camp
Each representation reflects the cultural viewpoint and interests of the person producing it
questions.explanation: Representations of place are shaped by the values and interests of the people making them, so a digger seeking land and a community describing their Country produce very different accounts of the same place. The claim that eyewitness status makes the letter more accurate is tempting, but being present does not remove a writer's assumptions — the digger's phrase 'waiting to be claimed' reveals a viewpoint, not a fact. Ask whose interests each version serves.

questions.stem: In analysing how language features represent a perspective, what does the term 'connotation' refer to?
options: The degree of certainty a word gives a claim, such as 'might' or 'must'
The associations and feelings a word carries beyond its literal meaning
The plain dictionary meaning of a word, stripped of any associations
The repetition of a consonant sound across words placed close together
questions.explanation: Connotation is the extra layer of association a word carries, which is why 'mob' and 'gathering' can name the same group yet position readers differently. The plain dictionary meaning is denotation, and confusing the two is the most common slip — denotation is what a word points to, connotation is what it makes you feel. The other options define alliteration and modality, which are separate features. Cue: if the question is about attitude created by word choice, it is connotation.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses high modality to present the writer's perspective as certain?
options: The council might consider repairing the crossing at some stage.
Perhaps the council could look again at the crossing next year.
The council may possibly repair the crossing after the wet season.
The council must repair the crossing before the school term begins.
questions.explanation: High modality words such as 'must', 'will' and 'clearly' present a claim as certain or obligatory, which strengthens the writer's stance. The option using 'might consider' is tempting because it sounds formal and official, but 'might' is low modality and leaves the action open. Cue: test the modal word alone — 'must' commits, while 'might', 'could' and 'may possibly' hedge.
questions.teaching:
Modality is how certain or obliged a statement sounds, and writers adjust it deliberately.

High modality — must, will, certainly, never — presents a claim as beyond question and is the language of demands and strong recommendations. Low modality — might, could, perhaps, sometimes — leaves room for doubt and is the language of careful academic writing. Neither is better; they suit different purposes. Spotting which a writer has chosen tells you how firmly they want their position taken, and often how much evidence they actually have.

questions.stem: In a persuasive article, why does a writer usually attribute a quotation to a named expert such as a river ecologist?
options: To prove the claim is true, since quoted words cannot be disputed
To remove the writer's own perspective and make the text fully neutral
To show the writer is uncertain and is passing responsibility to someone else
To lend authority to the claim by showing an informed source supports it
questions.explanation: Naming a credible source borrows that person's standing, so readers are more likely to accept the surrounding claim — that is why attribution is a persuasive choice, not just a courtesy. The idea that a quotation proves the claim is tempting, but a quotation only shows that someone said something; the source's expertise, date and context still have to be weighed. A quotation is also selected by the writer, so it carries the writer's perspective rather than erasing it.

questions.stem: A company media release states: 'The wetland was cleared and several hundred trees were lost.' What perspective does this construction create?
options: It suggests uncertainty about whether the clearing happened at all
It moves the event into the future, presenting it as a possible risk
It leaves out who acted, so responsibility for the clearing is obscured
It names those responsible directly, which makes the admission stronger
questions.explanation: These are agentless passive constructions: the actions are reported but the actor is never named, so the events read almost like weather rather than decisions. The option about naming those responsible reverses the effect — an active version such as 'we cleared the wetland' would do that. Cue: after a passive verb, look for 'by whom'; if it is missing, ask whose interests that serves.

questions.stem: A 2024 opinion piece argues that secondary students today cannot concentrate because of phones. Its only evidence is a 2004 survey of 30 university students. Which evaluation of this source is strongest?
options: The source is strong because an older study has had longer to be checked by others
The source is irrelevant because opinion pieces should not rely on research at all
The source is weak here: it is dated, very small and drawn from a different age group
The source is strong because surveys always produce objective numerical evidence
questions.explanation: Evaluating a source means testing its date, size and fit to the claim, and this survey fails all three: it predates smartphones, samples only 30 people and studies university rather than secondary students. The claim that surveys are always objective is tempting because numbers look authoritative, but sample size and question design shape the result. Cue: match the source to the exact claim it is being used to support.

questions.stem: A scientist writes: 'In extreme drought years, the river may fall below minimum flow.' A campaign flyer prints: 'Scientists say the river is falling below minimum flow.' What has the flyer done to the source?
options: It has kept the meaning intact, since 'may fall' and 'is falling' both describe low water levels
It has weakened the original warning by dropping the word 'extreme', making the situation sound milder
It has altered only the tense, which does not change how certain the statement sounds to readers
It has cut the condition and lowered the hedging, turning a qualified possibility into a present certainty
questions.explanation: The original claim is doubly limited — by the condition 'in extreme drought years' and by the low-modality verb 'may fall'. Removing both converts a conditional prediction into a statement of fact, which is a misuse of the source even though the topic is unchanged. The 'meaning intact' option is the trap: a possibility and an ongoing event are different claims, so the same subject matter does not mean the same assertion. Cue: when a quotation is repurposed, check the modal verbs and any 'if/when' conditions first.

questions.stem: A narrative opens with a woman standing at an airport gate, then moves back three years to the events that brought her there, before returning to the airport at the end. What structural technique is being used?
options: Parallel plotting, because two separate storylines run at the same time throughout
Cause and effect ordering, because every event is presented in the order it occurred
Flashback within a frame, so the earlier events are read in light of the opening scene
Foreshadowing, because the opening scene hints at events that have not yet happened
questions.explanation: The opening and closing airport scenes frame a section set earlier in time, which is a flashback: the reader already knows where the story ends up, so the earlier events carry extra weight. Foreshadowing is tempting, but foreshadowing only hints at what is coming, whereas here the text actually narrates a whole earlier period in detail. If the text moves back and tells the earlier events, it is flashback; if it merely drops a hint, it is foreshadowing.

questions.stem: An article about traffic congestion is organised as: description of the problem, its causes, then three possible solutions. What is this organisational pattern called?
options: Compare and contrast
Chronological recount
Alphabetical classification
Problem and solution
questions.explanation: A problem-solution structure sets out an issue and its causes, then proposes ways of addressing it, which is exactly the sequence described. Compare and contrast is the wrong label because the article does not weigh two subjects against each other; the three solutions are proposals, not items being compared with a rival. Look at what the sections are doing overall rather than at how many items appear in one section.
questions.teaching:
Texts are organised in recognisable patterns, and identifying the pattern helps you follow and remember the content.

Chronological order runs through time. Compare and contrast sets two things against each other. Cause and effect traces consequences. Description organises by feature. And one pattern sets out a difficulty, explores why it exists, and then proposes ways of dealing with it. Recognising the shape from the sequence of sections is what the question asks — so look at what each part of the text is doing rather than what it is about.

questions.stem: Why do writers of persuasive texts often place their strongest argument last rather than in the middle?
options: The final position is the most memorable, so the reader is left holding the strongest reason
Readers usually stop paying attention after the first paragraph, so weak points belong early
The last argument does not need evidence, because the conclusion follows immediately after
Placing a strong argument early would make the writer sound biased to the reader
questions.explanation: Order shapes emphasis: ideas at the end of a text sit closest to the conclusion and stay with the reader, so building towards the strongest point makes the case feel like it is gaining force. The claim that readers stop paying attention after the first paragraph is false — openings are highly emphatic positions too, which is why many writers also place a strong point there. The general principle is that beginnings and endings carry the most weight, and writers choose accordingly.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cohesive device that signals a contrast between two ideas in adjoining sentences?
options: 'However' at the start of the second sentence
'Furthermore' at the start of the second sentence
'For instance' at the start of the second sentence
'Consequently' at the start of the second sentence
questions.explanation: Connectives carry specific relationships, and 'however' marks a contrast or concession between what came before and what follows. 'Consequently' is a common wrong pick, but it signals a result flowing from the previous idea, not a contrast with it. Sort connectives by the relationship they name: adding, contrasting, exemplifying or showing cause.
questions.teaching:
Cohesive devices are the words that tie sentences together, and they come in kinds according to the relationship they signal.

Some add — furthermore, in addition, also. Some sequence — first, next, finally. Some show cause — therefore, consequently, as a result. Some give examples. And some signal that what follows will run against what came before, warning the reader to expect a turn. Matching the connective to the relationship being signalled is the skill, and using the wrong kind actively misleads a reader.

questions.stem: Two students analyse the same feature article. One writes that the writer 'delays naming the factory until paragraph six'. Which comment turns that observation into an analysis of how organisation shapes meaning?
options: By that point the reader already sympathises with the residents, so the naming lands as an accusation
The delay shows the writer has organised the article into six clear paragraphs of similar length
The delay proves the writer is uncertain about the facts and is avoiding naming the company
Naming things late is a standard feature of feature articles, so the choice carries no meaning
questions.explanation: Analysis of structure explains the effect of a choice on the reader at that point in the text, which is what linking the delayed naming to the reader's built-up sympathy does. Saying the delay proves uncertainty is wrong because the writer does name the factory, and does so at a point of maximum impact — the choice is emphatic, not evasive. The test for structural analysis is whether you have said what the reader thinks or feels because of the ordering.

questions.stem: An online explainer on plastic waste uses subheadings such as 'Where it comes from', 'Where it ends up' and 'What you can do'. How do these subheadings shape meaning for the reader?
options: They divide the topic into stages and lead the reader towards action as the final stage
They summarise the writer's argument so the body paragraphs are not needed
They allow the reader to skip sections without losing any of the writer's meaning
They show the text is neutral, because subheadings cannot express a point of view
questions.explanation: Subheadings do more than break up a page: their sequence maps a path through the topic, and ending on 'What you can do' positions personal action as the outcome of everything explained before it. The idea that a reader can skip sections and lose nothing is false — the order builds understanding, so the final section only makes sense after the earlier causes are established. Read the subheadings as a list and ask what journey they take the reader on.

questions.stem: A reader pauses and thinks, 'I've lost track of who is speaking here — I'll reread the last two paragraphs.' Which comprehension strategy is this?
options: Connecting
Summarising
Monitoring
Visualising
questions.explanation: Monitoring is checking your own understanding as you read and taking action, such as rereading, when meaning breaks down. Visualising is tempting because rereading may help build a picture, but visualising specifically means forming mental images of what the text describes, not noticing a comprehension breakdown. The cue for monitoring is that the reader's attention turns to their own understanding.
questions.teaching:
Good readers do several things automatically, and comprehension strategies are those habits made explicit.

Predicting guesses what comes next. Questioning asks things of the text. Summarising condenses. Visualising builds a mental picture. Connecting links the text to what you already know. And one strategy is about noticing your own understanding — realising you have stopped following, and doing something about it by rereading, slowing down or looking something up. It is the one that involves watching yourself read rather than working on the text.

questions.stem: A feature article on housing opens: 'Kalinda has moved four times in three years. She keeps her plates in a box.' Which inference is best supported by these lines?
options: Kalinda dislikes cooking and rarely eats at home
Kalinda has been evicted by landlords on each occasion
Kalinda has recently arrived in Australia from overseas
Kalinda expects to move again and lives without settling in
questions.explanation: Keeping plates packed is a detail that only makes sense if another move is anticipated, so the supported inference is about impermanence. The claim about evictions is tempting because frequent moves suggest instability, but the text names no cause for the moves, so this goes beyond the evidence. The test of a good inference is that you can point to the words that force it.

questions.stem: Reading a feature article about a family evacuating during a bushfire, Aleisha writes in the margin: 'This is like the flood chapter in the novel we studied — both show ordinary routines breaking down first.' Which comprehension strategy is she using?
options: Connecting, because she is relating this text to another text that handles a similar idea
Visualising, because she is imagining the family's street as the fire front approaches
Predicting, because she is working out what the article will describe in its later sections
Summarising, because she is reducing the article's content to a single main idea
questions.explanation: Connecting means relating a text to your own experience, to the wider world, or to another text, in order to interpret its ideas — here a text-to-text link about how disaster writing works. Summarising is the most tempting alternative because her note is short, but a summary must state what this article says, whereas her note reaches outside it to a different text. The cue for connecting is the comparison word: 'like', 'reminds me of', 'the same as in'.

questions.stem: Read these lines: 'Nan never says anything about the photographs. She dusts the frames every Sunday, and turns the largest one face down when visitors arrive.' Which inference is best supported?
options: Visitors to the house have asked Nan to hide the largest photograph because it upsets them
Nan values the largest photograph but wants the memory attached to it kept private from visitors
Nan dislikes having photographs in the house and would prefer that all of them were removed
Nan can no longer remember who the people in the photographs are, so she avoids the subject
questions.explanation: Inferring means combining stated details with reasoning to reach a conclusion the text supports but does not state: the weekly dusting shows care, while turning it down for visitors shows a wish for privacy, so both details are accounted for. The claim that she dislikes the photographs is tempting because of her silence, but it is contradicted by the dusting, and a good inference must fit every detail rather than just one. The other two options invent information — memory loss and a visitor's request — that the passage gives no basis for.

questions.stem: While reading a description of a flooded main street, a student deliberately builds a picture in her mind of the muddy water, the sandbags and the abandoned shopping trolley. Which comprehension strategy is she using?
options: Predicting — using clues to work out what will happen next
Monitoring — noticing when her understanding has broken down
Summarising — reducing the passage to its main ideas in a few words
Visualising — turning the text's descriptive detail into mental images
questions.explanation: Visualising means constructing sensory mental images from the details a text supplies, which helps a reader hold and interpret information. Predicting is the tempting choice because both involve the reader's mind going beyond the words, but predicting is about forecasting what comes next, and here she is picturing what is already described. The cue: if the reader is seeing the scene on the page, it is visualising; if she is guessing the page ahead, it is predicting.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks for a summary of a two-page article on food waste. What does summarising require you to do?
options: Add your own judgement about whether the writer's argument is convincing
Explain each paragraph in more detail than the article itself gives
State the article's main ideas briefly in your own words, leaving out minor detail
Copy the article's three most striking sentences in the order they appear
questions.explanation: A summary compresses a text: it keeps the central ideas, drops examples and side detail, and is written in the reader's own words. Copying striking sentences is quoting, not summarising, because selecting vivid lines does not guarantee they carry the main ideas. Remember that a summary should be shorter than the original and reproduce no one's wording but your own.

questions.stem: Before reading, a student sees an article titled 'The last bus' with the subheadings 'Routes cut', 'Who is stranded' and 'What council says'. Which of these is a prediction properly grounded in those text features?
options: Public transport funding in outer suburbs is a serious problem that needs fixing
The word 'stranded' suggests people left without options, which sounds quite negative
The article will probably explain reduced bus services and their effect on residents
The article states that council has cancelled several routes across the outer suburbs
questions.explanation: Predicting means using available cues — title, subheadings, images — to form a testable expectation about content that you then confirm or revise while reading. The statement that council has cancelled routes is tempting but it is written as an established fact drawn from the text, and the student has not read the article yet, so it is not a prediction. A prediction is signalled by tentative wording such as 'probably' or 'is likely to', and it points forward to what is still unread.

questions.stem: After reading an opinion piece claiming 'phone bans have transformed learning', a student writes four questions. Which one best moves beyond locating information to evaluating the writer's ideas?
options: In which year was the trial at the two schools first introduced?
What does the writer mean by 'transformed' in the opening sentence?
How many benefits of the phone ban does the writer list in total?
Do results from two trial schools really justify a claim about all schools?
questions.explanation: Evaluative questioning interrogates the strength of the link between a writer's evidence and their claim, rather than retrieving or clarifying content. Asking what 'transformed' means is tempting because it does require thinking, but it is a clarifying question about word meaning, which supports comprehension without judging the argument. The cue: evaluation asks whether the text's ideas hold up; retrieval and clarification only ask what the text says.

questions.stem: A student is writing a text that 'raises an issue' about litter in the school grounds. What does raising an issue mainly require the text to do?
options: Describe the setting in vivid sensory detail for enjoyment
Identify a problem and make readers see why it matters
Retell the events of a single day in chronological order
List every fact discovered during research without comment
questions.explanation: A text that raises an issue names a problem and establishes its significance for a particular audience, so readers accept there is something to address. Retelling events in order is the work of a report or recount, which records what happened rather than arguing that it matters. The cue is the word 'issue': it points to a problem plus a reason to care, not just information.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a multimodal element a student could add to a digital text on water use?
options: A concluding paragraph that restates the main argument
A series of rhetorical questions addressed to the reader
An interactive graph showing household water use by month
A topic sentence at the start of each body paragraph
questions.explanation: Multimodal elements combine modes beyond written words, such as image, sound, movement or interactive visuals, so an interactive graph qualifies. 'A series of rhetorical questions' is tempting because it feels like a special technique, but it is still purely written or spoken language in one mode. Check whether the feature adds a different mode, not just a different device.
questions.teaching:
A multimodal text combines more than one channel of communication, and digital texts make that easy.

Modes include written words, spoken words, still images, moving images, sound and layout. Adding any of these alongside the writing makes a text multimodal, and something the reader can manipulate adds a further dimension again. The point of analysing them is that meaning comes from how the modes work together — a graph can make a pattern instantly visible that a paragraph would take a page to describe.

questions.stem: Nadia is writing a letter to her local council advancing the opinion that a skate park should be built. Which sentence uses language most deliberately for that purpose and audience?
options: Last Saturday I met my cousin at the shops and we talked about skating for ages.
Council has a real chance here to give young residents somewhere safe and supervised to go.
Skate parks are usually made of concrete and often include ramps, rails and bowls.
Heaps of us are totally over having nowhere to skate around this dead-boring suburb.
questions.explanation: Advancing an opinion to a council means framing the proposal as a benefit the council can deliver, using respectful, reasoned wording aimed at decision-makers. The informal complaint about a 'dead-boring suburb' does express an opinion, but its slang and insult work against the audience and would weaken the case. Match register to the reader: councils respond to reasoned benefit, not venting.

questions.stem: A Year 8 class must present research on food waste as a short podcast episode rather than a written report. Which change to their text is most necessary because of the shift in mode?
options: Making the language much more formal, since audio texts require formal register
Cutting the conclusion, since podcasts end when the speakers run out of material
Adding spoken signposts and varying voice, since listeners cannot scan back over the text
Removing all statistics, since audiences cannot understand numbers when listening
questions.explanation: Listeners receive a spoken text in one pass and cannot reread, so clear verbal signposting and vocal variety carry the structure that headings and paragraphs carry in print. 'Making the language much more formal' is tempting because presentations feel formal, but audio texts often work better with conversational register; mode does not automatically raise formality. Ask what the audience physically can and cannot do with the text.

questions.stem: A Year 8 student is writing a news report of the school athletics carnival for the college newsletter. Which set of language and textual choices best suits a text whose purpose is to report events?
options: Third person, past tense, the key who/what/when/where in the opening, and quotes attributed to named students
First person throughout, present tense, and a closing paragraph explaining what the writer learned about themselves
Second person address, imperative verbs and numbered steps so readers can repeat each event themselves
Emotive adjectives, rhetorical questions and a call to action urging readers to agree with the writer
questions.explanation: Reporting events calls for an informative stance: the reader needs the essential facts early, verifiable detail, and other voices brought in through attributed quotes, which is why third person and past tense dominate. The option built on emotive adjectives, rhetorical questions and a call to action describes an opinion or persuasive text, not a report — those features exist to move the reader rather than inform them. The cue is the purpose word: 'report' means recount what happened and who said what; 'advance an opinion' means argue a position.

questions.stem: Two sentences are drafted about the same council decision. Which one belongs in a news report rather than an opinion piece?
options: Surely no reasonable councillor could have supported closing Marsden Street on Tuesday.
It is obvious that Tuesday's vote will be remembered as the worst decision of the year.
Council voted 6-3 on Tuesday to close the Marsden Street crossing from 1 March.
Council's reckless 6-3 vote on Tuesday shows how little it cares about our safety.
questions.explanation: A report presents verifiable detail — the vote count, the date, the decision — without evaluative language, leaving readers to judge. The version calling the vote 'reckless' is tempting because it also contains the accurate figures, but the adjective and the claim about what council 'cares' about are the writer's judgement, which shifts the text into opinion. Test each sentence by asking whether every word could be checked against a record; if adjectives like 'reckless' or phrases like 'it is obvious' remain, you are advancing an opinion.

questions.stem: Jarrah publishes an article on the school blog raising the issue of stormwater flooding at the front gate. Which use of hyperlinks best serves that purpose?
options: Linking to popular unrelated videos partway down so more readers stay on the page longer
Linking his claim about drain capacity to the council's published drainage report so readers can check it
Linking every second sentence to an online dictionary so readers can look up any unfamiliar word
Linking the headline back to the blog's own homepage so readers can browse other student articles
questions.explanation: Digital elements are chosen deliberately to serve purpose: in an issue-raising text, a hyperlink to a source lets readers verify evidence, which strengthens the writer's credibility on the issue. Linking the headline to the homepage is tempting because navigation links are common on blogs, but that is site design, not a choice that develops the argument about flooding. Ask of any digital element: does this help the reader understand or trust the issue being raised? If not, it is decoration.

questions.stem: Tomas is publishing a digital article on the school website raising the issue of unshaded areas in the junior yard. He includes a photograph of the bare asphalt yard taken at lunchtime. Which caption best makes the image do argumentative work alongside his written text?
options: 'A photograph of the school's junior yard, taken by the author on a Tuesday in February.'
'Everyone agrees this is easily the worst and most neglected schoolyard in the whole state.'
'The junior yard is a large open area where many students choose to spend their lunchtimes.'
'At 12.30pm in February, the only shade in the junior yard is a two-metre strip beside the fence.'
questions.explanation: A caption in a multimodal text should add information that the image alone cannot give and tie it to the argument — here the time, season and the measured extent of shade turn the photograph into evidence that the yard is unshaded when students use it. The most tempting choice is the neutral label naming the author and date: it identifies the image but adds nothing that advances the issue, so the photograph stays decorative. The cue is to ask whether the caption gives the reader a fact that strengthens the claim; unsupported hyperbole about the 'worst in the state' and vague general description both fail that test.

questions.stem: Which of these changes to a draft feature article is a revision change rather than an editing change?
options: Correcting the spelling of 'seperate' to 'separate' in the closing sentence
Moving the paragraph on causes so that it comes before the paragraph on effects
Changing 'there boots' to 'their boots' in the second paragraph of the article
Inserting a missing comma after the introductory phrase 'By Friday afternoon'
questions.explanation: Resequencing paragraphs changes how the reader follows the argument, which is a revision decision about structure and clarity. The homophone fix, the comma and the spelling correction are all surface-level edits: they make the text accurate but leave the ideas and their order untouched. Cue: if the change alters what the reader understands or the order they meet ideas in, it is revision.

questions.stem: A student's draft reads: 'The thing about the canteen is that it is kind of a problem for a lot of students at lunchtime.' Which redraft best refines and clarifies the idea?
options: 'The canteen, which is located near the gym, is used by students at lunchtime every school day.'
'Canteen queues regularly run for twenty minutes, so many students return to class without eating.'
'The thing about the canteen is that it is honestly a really big problem for so many students.'
'The canteen situation at lunchtime is something that concerns a significant proportion of students.'
questions.explanation: Refining an idea means replacing vague fillers ('the thing about', 'kind of', 'a problem') with specific detail that shows the reader exactly what the problem is and what it causes. The version using 'a significant proportion of students' is tempting because it sounds more formal, but formality is not clarity — it still never says what the problem actually is. Cue: ask what a reader could now picture or measure that they could not before.

questions.stem: A paragraph argues that the school should plant shade trees. Its four sentences are: (1) topic sentence on heat in the yard; (2) temperature data from summer; (3) a sentence about the canteen's new menu; (4) a concluding link to the cost of trees. Which edit best improves the paragraph's coherence?
options: Delete sentence 3, because it introduces a topic unrelated to the paragraph's controlling idea
Move sentence 3 to the start, so the paragraph opens with a concrete detail about school life
Add a connective such as 'similarly' before sentence 3 to link it to the temperature data
Split the paragraph after sentence 2 so that each idea is given its own short paragraph
questions.explanation: A coherent paragraph develops one controlling idea, so material that belongs to a different topic weakens it no matter where it sits. Adding 'similarly' is the tempting fix because connectives usually improve flow, but a connective cannot create a real relationship between shade trees and a canteen menu — it only disguises the gap. Cue: check each sentence against the topic sentence before reaching for a linking word.

questions.stem: Two students give feedback on the same classmate's persuasive draft. Which comment is most likely to help the writer refine and clarify their ideas?
options: 'I really enjoyed reading this and I think your argument is going to convince most people.'
'There are three spelling mistakes in paragraph two and a comma missing in your final line.'
'This is much better than your last piece, so I wouldn't change anything at all before you submit.'
'Your second reason isn't backed by evidence — could you add the survey figure you mentioned in class?'
questions.explanation: Useful revision feedback is specific, points to a particular part of the text, and suggests an action the writer can take on the ideas themselves. The spelling and comma comment is tempting because it is specific and accurate, but it is proofreading feedback and does nothing to strengthen the argument. Cue: ask whether the comment tells the writer what to change and why it would improve the reader's understanding.

questions.stem: Which of these post-writing statements best demonstrates genuine reflection on the reviewing and editing process?
options: 'My partner said the introduction was confusing, so I rewrote it the way she suggested word for word.'
'Reading my draft aloud showed me two rambling sentences, so I now use that check before I hand anything in.'
'I read my whole piece through twice at the end and I fixed all the mistakes that I could find in it.'
'I worked hard on this piece and spent much longer editing it than I did on my last assessment task.'
questions.explanation: Reflection names a specific strategy, states what it revealed about the text, and draws a conclusion the writer can carry forward — that is what makes it reflection rather than description. The statement about reading through twice and fixing mistakes is tempting because it describes real editing, but it only reports activity; it identifies no strategy, no insight and no future use. Cue: look for strategy plus effect plus what I will do next time.

questions.stem: A draft reads: 'The council told the school it would pay for the new crossing, which annoyed some parents.' Which redraft best clarifies the idea?
options: 'The council told the school that the school would pay for the new crossing, and this decision annoyed some parents.'
'The council told the school it would definitely pay for the new crossing, which really annoyed some parents.'
'The council told the school it would pay for the new crossing. This annoyed some parents very much.'
'Annoyingly for parents, the council told the school it would pay for the brand-new pedestrian crossing.'
questions.explanation: The problem is ambiguous reference: 'it' could mean the council or the school, and 'which' could point to the payment or the whole announcement. The clearest redraft names who is paying and replaces 'which' with a phrase that states what annoyed parents. The version that splits the sentence in two is tempting because shorter sentences look clearer, but 'it' and 'This' remain just as ambiguous. When revising for clarity, check every pronoun has one possible referent rather than simply shortening sentences.

questions.stem: Which of these is an 'implied' meaning of a text rather than a stated one?
options: A meaning the writer sets out directly in a topic sentence or headline
A meaning found in the caption printed underneath a photograph
A meaning that appears in a quotation attributed to a named expert
A meaning the reader works out from clues, word choice or what is left out
questions.explanation: Implied meanings are not written on the page; readers infer them from details, connotations, emphasis and omissions. A meaning set out directly in a topic sentence is the clearest example of a stated meaning, which is why that option is tempting but wrong. If you can quote a sentence that says it, it is stated; if you must reason towards it, it is implied.

questions.stem: During a small-group discussion, which contribution best supports another student's interpretation of a text?
options: 'That's a good point because Sam usually gets these questions right in class.'
'I agree, and I also think the writer used too many long sentences.'
'I agree — and the line about the empty desk shows the loss you mentioned.'
'I agree with everything Sam said, so I don't really need to add anything.'
questions.explanation: Supporting an interpretation means adding weight to it, usually with further evidence from the text that shows why the reading holds. Simply agreeing with everything said adds nothing to the group's thinking, even though it sounds cooperative. Relying on a classmate's reputation is an appeal to the person, not to the text — support must come from the words on the page.

questions.stem: A Year 8 class is holding a formal panel discussion for an audience of parents, rather than a casual group chat. Which adjustment to interaction skills is most necessary?
options: Speak in complete sentences, signpost each point and avoid slang and in-jokes
Speak faster to fit more points into the time given for the panel
Avoid disagreeing with other panel members while parents are listening
Read the whole contribution word for word from a printed script
questions.explanation: Purpose and context shape how you interact: a formal panel with an unfamiliar audience calls for clearer structure, signposting and language that outsiders can follow. Avoiding all disagreement is wrong because a panel exists to test ideas — disagreement is expected, just handled courteously. Ask what the audience needs to follow you, not how to say the most.

questions.stem: Which question asked in a discussion does the most to test whether a classmate's claim about a text is supported?
options: 'Has anyone else in the group also thought the writer sounded angry?'
'Would you feel angry if that had happened in your own suburb?'
'Which part of the article made you read the writer's tone as angry?'
'Do you honestly believe the writer of that article was angry?'
questions.explanation: Asking which part of the text produced the reading pushes the speaker back to evidence, which is how a discussion tests an interpretation. Asking whether others thought the same only measures popularity, not support, so agreement in the group would prove nothing about the text. Effective probing questions point at the page, not at feelings or numbers.

questions.stem: A student says: 'The writer clearly thinks the council is incompetent, even though she never says so.' Which response best challenges this as an interpretation of implied meaning?
options: 'The words she uses about the council are neutral — which details led you there?'
'She never says it, so the text cannot imply anything about the council at all.'
'You can't know what a writer thinks, so no one should claim implied meanings.'
'I think the council is actually incompetent, so her article seems fair to me.'
questions.explanation: A strong challenge to an inference tests whether the text's details actually support it, so pointing to neutral word choice and asking for the evidence keeps the discussion on the text. Claiming that an unstated idea cannot be implied is simply false — implication is how texts convey attitude without stating it. Notice the difference between denying that implication exists and questioning whether this particular implication is supported.

questions.stem: Mid-discussion, a group realises two students are using the word 'biased' to mean different things. What is the most useful interaction move at this point?
options: Drop the word 'biased' and avoid discussing the writer's perspective
Pause to agree on what 'biased' will mean for this discussion, then continue
Let each student keep their own meaning so the discussion is not interrupted
Vote on whose definition of 'biased' the group prefers to use
questions.explanation: When a key term is being used in two ways, the group is no longer arguing about the same thing, so clarifying the term is what makes any support or challenge meaningful. Letting each student keep a private meaning feels efficient but guarantees the disagreement is only verbal. Voting decides preference, not meaning, and abandoning the word removes an idea the discussion needs.

questions.stem: In a group discussion about a text, what does it mean to 'build on' another student's contribution?
options: Politely disagreeing with their point and explaining why your reading is better
Extending their point by adding evidence from the text or taking their idea a step further
Restating their point in slightly different words so the group has time to think
Introducing the separate point you had prepared before the discussion began
questions.explanation: Building on a contribution means treating it as a starting point and adding something to it — further textual evidence, a consequence, or a refinement — so the group's thinking moves forward. Restating the point in different words is paraphrasing: it shows you listened, but it adds no new idea, which is why it is not building on the point. Politely disagreeing is challenging, not building. The cue is direction: building extends the same idea, challenging pushes back on it, and paraphrasing simply repeats it.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of voice a speaker can control while delivering a spoken presentation?
options: Pace — deliberately slowing down when stating a key statistic
Font — choosing a bold sans-serif for the slide headings
Layout — arranging images in a grid on each slide
Paragraphing — starting a new block of text for each idea
questions.explanation: Features of voice are the vocal choices a speaker makes as they speak: pace, volume, pitch, tone, emphasis and pause. Slowing down on a key statistic is a pace choice, so it is a feature of voice. Choosing a bold font is tempting because it also creates emphasis, but it is a visual or multimodal design element of the slides, not something done with the voice. The cue is to ask whether the audience hears the choice or sees it.
questions.teaching:
Delivering a presentation involves choices about the voice that are separate from the words themselves.

The controllable features include how loudly you speak, how high or low, how much you stress particular words, where you pause, and how fast you go. Each can be used deliberately: slowing down signals importance, pausing lets a point land, raising volume marks a climax. Note the question asks for something the speaker controls with their voice — gestures and slides are delivery choices too, but they are not vocal ones.

questions.stem: Ben is delivering a five-minute proposal to the school council — a formal audience — arguing for longer library opening hours. Which choice would most clearly give his spoken text the structure that suits this context?
options: Keeping his voice at one flat pitch and volume so the audience attends to content, not delivery
Reading his written research report aloud word for word, since the ideas are already organised
Listing as many statistics as he can without explaining them, so the talk sounds authoritative
Previewing his three main points at the start, then naming each one aloud as he moves to it
questions.explanation: Listeners cannot re-read a spoken text, so structure has to be made audible: an opening preview and spoken signposts at each transition let the audience track where the argument is going. Reading the written report aloud word for word is the most tempting alternative because the ideas are indeed organised, but written organisation relies on paragraphs, headings and rereading — a listener gets none of those, so the text must be reshaped for the spoken mode. The cue is to ask whether the structure can be *heard*: if it only works on the page, it needs signposting.
